title: Lesson 13: Reference Architectures and Internal Tooling That Compound
description: How a practice harvests the reusable architecture and internal tooling that each engagement leaves behind, so the marginal cost of repeated work falls and the firm compounds.

questions.question: When should a practice write down a reference architecture?
options: As soon as it decides to offer a class of work, so the first engagement can follow it.
After the second or third time it has done that kind of work, once the shape has repeated.
Only after a client asks for a formal methodology document.
Whenever a competitor publishes an equivalent pattern for the same problem.
questions.explanation: A pattern is only trustworthy once it has been earned by repetition, so a premature reference architecture is confident and wrong.

questions.question: Which three properties separate compounding internal tooling from a one-off expense?
options: It is fast, cheap, and fully automated.
It is documented, approved, and version controlled.
It is reused, improves with use, and has a named owner.
It is generic, portable, and independent of any single client.
questions.explanation: Tooling compounds only when it is reused, improves with each use, and has a named owner to keep it current.

questions.question: What is the failure mode of accumulated machinery that is never reviewed?
options: It outlives its accuracy, so a stale pattern is trusted and followed with confidence.
It grows faster than the practice can document it.
It becomes too specific to the clients it was built for.
It discourages the team from solving new problems from first principles.
questions.explanation: A stale pattern is worse than no pattern because it is trusted, so each asset needs an owner and a review cadence.
